analysis.one_liner: Strips federal Clean Water Act protection from most wetlands, streams, and seasonal waterways nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have removed Clean Water Act protections from most wetlands and streams that lack a continuous connection to navigable waters, died in committee without a single hearing, vote, or cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the 2015 Clean Water Rule, the regulation that decides which waters and wetlands the federal government can protect from pollution and destruction. It would then write a much narrower definition into law: only bodies of water you can boat on, and permanent streams, rivers, and lakes connected to them, would count. Most wetlands, dry washes, and streams that flow only after rain would lose federal pollution protection entirely. The bill was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, farmers, real estate developers, energy companies, and mining operators would have gained: hundreds of thousands of streams and millions of acres of wetlands would have dropped out of federal permitting, so filling a wetland or discharging into a seasonal stream would no longer require a Clean Water Act permit. Landowners who felt the 2015 rule was overbroad would have had a permanent, court-proof definition written into the statute itself.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, farm operators, energy and mining firms

how_it_helps.text: It nullifies the 2015 Clean Water Rule, which had defined which waters the EPA and Army Corps regulate, and replaces it with a much shorter statutory list of protected waters.

It excludes wetlands such as prairie potholes, vernal pools, and playa lakes that lack a continuous surface connection to navigable waters, along with channels that flow intermittently or ephemerally, from federal jurisdiction.
It bars regulators from treating scattered wetlands as a collective system when deciding whether they are protected, a method the 2015 rule relied on.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on everyone who depends on clean water: smaller streams and wetlands filter pollution, store floodwater, and feed drinking-water supplies, and the bill would have allowed them to be filled, drained, or polluted without federal review. State environmental agencies would have picked up more of the enforcement burden with their own budgets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and states relying on clean water

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued the 2015 Clean Water Rule reached too far, subjecting ordinary farm ponds, ditches, and dry land to federal permits and litigation, and that a statutory definition would give landowners certainty that agency rules could not change with each administration.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill excluded wetlands and seasonal streams that science shows affect downstream water quality, and that it would have removed federal pollution protections entirely from those waters, leaving them to whatever state rules exist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real regulatory relief to landowners who faced federal permitting for marginal waters, but it did so by removing pollution protections from most of the nation's wetlands and seasonal streams in one stroke, with no transition for states that would inherit the burden. Because it never advanced, no one actually gained or lost anything from it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced, bounced to a water subcommittee the next day, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Thornberry introduced the bill on April 10, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress with no further action.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its entire life and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, which favored the public's current legal position: the broad Clean Water Act jurisdiction in place under statute stayed intact, and the industries hoping for a permanent statutory rollback of water protections got nothing. The bill's single sponsor also gained nothing beyond having made a statement.

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 2015 Clean Water Rule and narrow the Clean Water Act's jurisdiction by statute.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee from April 2019 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill's lone sponsor was a Republican with no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted most wetlands from federal permitting, cutting the cost and delay of building on wet land. The public cost is loss of wetlands that absorb floods and filter water.

Farmers would have been freed from federal permitting over farm ponds, ditches, and prairie pothole wetlands, a frequent complaint about the 2015 rule. Some of that relief comes at the expense of downstream water quality.
Discharges into seasonal streams and isolated wetlands would no longer need Clean Water Act permits, lowering compliance costs for pipelines, mining, and extraction projects near smaller waters.

industries.industry: Municipal water utilities and downstream water users
industries.note: Smaller streams and wetlands feed the rivers and reservoirs cities drink from; removing them from protection would raise treatment and flooding costs for ratepayers.
